items.subtype_name: How does Text 2 relate to Text 1?
items.stimulus:
Text 1
In trials at forty accounting and software firms, employees moved to a four-day week with no cut in pay. Managers reported that output held steady while sick days and reported burnout fell. Advocates concluded that a shorter week benefits workers and employers alike.

Text 2
The office trials are encouraging, but they may not describe every workplace. When a regional hospital laundry tried the same schedule, its machines still needed staff every day, so the remaining shifts grew longer and output fell by nearly a tenth.
items.stem: Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?
choices: It identifies a workplace where the result reported in Text 1 did not hold.
It offers further evidence that output held steady under a shorter week.
It argues that a four-day week reduces output in nearly every kind of job.
It describes the office trials that the advocates in Text 1 had criticized.
items.explanation: Text 1 reports a general result: at office firms, output held steady under a four-day week, and advocates say everyone benefits. Text 2 starts by crediting those trials ("encouraging"), then turns to one workplace, a hospital laundry, where output fell. So Text 2 limits the scope of Text 1's claim without rejecting it.

B.why: You picked up the shared topic but missed the turn at "but." At the laundry output fell, so Text 2 does not support the steady-output finding.

C.why: You turned one counterexample into a sweeping rule. Text 2 describes one laundry and calls the office results encouraging, so it never says nearly every job loses output.

D.why: You assigned the wrong role to Text 1. The advocates praised the office trials and did not criticize them. This choice gets Text 2's subject right and Text 1's position wrong.

items.subtype_name: How does Text 2 relate to Text 1?
items.stimulus:
Text 1
Between 2015 and 2020, twelve towns installed chilled water fountains in their public parks. Over the same period, surveys showed that children in those towns drank about a third less soda. The researchers therefore concluded that easy access to free water led children to choose it over sugary drinks.

Text 2
No one doubts that soda drinking fell in these towns. Yet most of them also banned soda sales in their schools during those years, and that policy could simply have produced the drop on its own.
items.stem: Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?
choices: It questions whether soda drinking among the children actually declined.
It proposes a different possible cause for the decline described in Text 1.
It presents survey results showing that the fountains raised soda drinking.
It explains the method the researchers in Text 1 used to survey children.
items.explanation: Text 1 ends with its conclusion ("therefore"): the fountains caused the decline. Text 2 accepts that the decline happened ("No one doubts..."). It then names another explanation, the school soda bans, that "could simply" account for the same result. Text 2 agrees on the observation and offers a different cause.

A.why: You read Text 2 as disagreeing about everything. Its first sentence grants that soda drinking fell. It disputes only the cause.

C.why: You invented a finding that reverses both texts. Neither text reports that soda drinking rose, and Text 2 presents no new survey.

D.why: You fixed on the word "surveys" in Text 1. Text 2 never discusses how the data were gathered. It is about what caused the drop.

items.subtype_name: How does Text 2 relate to Text 1?

Text 1
Many astronomers think that "hot Jupiters," giant planets that orbit extremely close to their stars, could not have formed there, since too little gas exists so near a star. Instead, these planets are thought to have formed far out and then migrated inward over millions of years.

Text 2

items.stem: Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?
choices: It presents a general theory that the planet discussed in Text 1 illustrates.
It describes a planet that appears to have formed close to its own star.
It gives a specific example that is consistent with the view in Text 1.
It explains why astronomers first began searching for giant planets.
items.explanation: Text 1 states a general view: hot Jupiters formed far out and migrated inward. Text 2 describes one planet, WR-208b ("a telling case"), whose tilted orbit is what a long inward journey would produce. Text 2 is a specific example that supports Text 1's general claim.

Text 1
Seismologists have long cautioned that earthquakes cannot be predicted with any useful precision. Small tremors occur constantly, and only rarely does one turn out to be a foreshock to a major quake, so no one can say in advance when a large rupture will strike.

Text 2

items.stem: Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?

It claims that new sensors can now predict when large quakes will occur.
It gives an example of a small tremor that turned out to be a foreshock.
It rejects the alert sensors that the seismologists in Text 1 had recommended.
items.explanation: Text 2 opens with a concession ("Although the exact timing... remains beyond reach"), which agrees with Text 1 that quakes cannot be predicted. It extends the explanation in Text 1 to stories from an earlier period.

It argues that sailors' reports of sea serpents were largely accurate.

items.stimulus:
Text 1
In the early 1800s, English handloom weavers saw their earnings collapse. Many historians have traced this hardship to the power loom, which could produce several times as much cloth per worker as a handloom. Thus, they argue, the machine itself drove the weavers into poverty.

Text 2

items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?

Weavers' wages fell because too many workers entered the trade.
Power looms could produce cloth faster than handlooms could.
Few power looms were operating in England before the 1830s.

items.stimulus:
Text 1
Over the past four decades, weather forecasts have grown steadily more accurate. Satellites now track moisture and wind over oceans that once went unobserved, feeding richer data into forecasting models. A forecaster can therefore now plan a full week ahead with confidence.

Text 2

items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?

Forecasts are now dependable a week ahead for any kind of weather.
Satellite data has done little to improve forecasting models.
Thunderstorms have become harder to predict than they once were.

Static stretching before competition helps sprinters perform.

items.stimulus:
Text 1
In the eleven days before a magnitude 5.4 earthquake struck the Vessel Ridge fault, seismometers recorded over 300 small tremors clustered near the eventual rupture. Swarms on the Vessel Ridge fault reliably signal that a larger quake will follow.
The tremors were most likely connected to whatever produced the mainshock.
Rising fluid is the likelier source of the tremors recorded before the mainshock.

items.subtype_name: How does Text 2 relate to Text 1?
items.stimulus:
Text 1
After a wetland was restored upstream of Corbin in 2009, hydrologists compared fifteen storms from before and after the restoration. For storms of similar size, peak river flow at Corbin fell by an average of 20 percent. The team concluded that the wetland is an effective defense against flooding in the town.

Text 2
For storms like those fifteen, the wetland clearly helps. But none approached the size of Corbin's most destructive floods. In those, days of rain saturate the wetland before the peak arrives, leaving it little capacity to absorb more water.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: The restored wetland lowered peak river flow at Corbin during storms like those studied.
The restored wetland is an effective defense against all of the flooding Corbin experiences.
The fifteen storms studied included several of the largest floods in Corbin's history.
Wetlands upstream of a town become saturated during most heavy rainstorms.
items.explanation: Text 2 limits Text 1's claim to a smaller range of storms. It accepts the result for storms like the fifteen studied ('clearly helps') and denies it only for the largest floods. Both authors agree that the wetland reduced peak flow in storms of the kind that were measured.

B.why: You stretched Text 1's conclusion until it covered every flood. Text 2 says the wetland does little in the most destructive floods, so its author would reject this.

C.why: Text 2 says none of the fifteen storms approached the size of Corbin's worst floods.

D.why: Text 2 describes saturation only during the largest, multi-day storms. It does not say this happens in most heavy storms, and Text 1 never mentions saturation.

items.subtype_name: How does Text 2 relate to Text 1?
items.stimulus:
Text 1
During a 2021 marine heat wave, corals in Tavu Lagoon, where water temperatures swing by up to 6°C each day, bleached far less than corals on the nearby outer reef. Marine biologist Sione Fifita concluded that daily exposure to fluctuating temperatures had conditioned the lagoon corals to tolerate heat.

Text 2
It is difficult to exclude another route to the same result. Over many generations, the lagoon's temperature swings may have killed off heat-sensitive corals, leaving populations descended from tolerant survivors. On that view, an outer-reef coral moved into the lagoon would gain little.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: The lagoon's fluctuating temperatures help account for its corals' greater heat tolerance.
Individual corals grow more heat tolerant through daily exposure to temperature swings.
Outer-reef corals moved into Tavu Lagoon would gain little resistance to heat.
Lagoon corals and outer-reef corals bleached at similar rates during the heat wave.
items.explanation: Text 2 offers a different explanation for the same result, but both explanations depend on the temperature swings. In Text 1, the swings condition each coral. In Text 2, they remove sensitive corals over generations. Either way, the swings help explain the lagoon corals' tolerance.

B.why: This is Text 1's mechanism. Text 2 argues that a single coral moved into the lagoon would gain little, which goes directly against this claim.

C.why: This is the prediction from Text 2's view. Text 1's conditioning explanation suggests a moved coral would gain tolerance, so its author would not agree.

D.why: Text 1 reports that lagoon corals bleached far less, and Text 2 accepts that result ('the same result').
